obligations.text: Do not offer or use it; reliably block this output.

rules.note: Added by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744 (in force 27 Jul 2026); applies from 2 Dec 2026. Covered only where this output is the intended purpose or a reproducible outcome without adequate safeguards.

obligations.text: Do not sell, deploy or use this in the EU.

rules.title: Authorised real-time biometric identification for law enforcement

obligations.text: Get prior judicial or independent authorisation for each use.
Only use it where national law expressly allows it.
Complete a fundamental rights impact assessment and register the system before use.
Notify the market surveillance and data protection authorities.

rules.note: Excepted uses are permitted under strict conditions and the system is also Annex III high-risk (point 1(a)). Requires counsel.

rules.title: Safety component of a regulated product

obligations.text: Run a documented risk management process across the system's lifecycle.
Use relevant, representative training and test data and check it for bias.
Write technical documentation before release and keep it up to date.
Log events automatically so results can be traced.
Give deployers clear instructions for use.
Design it so a human can oversee it and stop it.
Make it accurate, robust and secure against attacks like data poisoning and prompt injection.
Run a quality management system.
Monitor it after release and report serious incidents.
Pass the product's conformity assessment, AI checks included.
Use it according to the provider's instructions.
Assign trained, competent people to oversee it.
Make sure the input data you control is relevant to the purpose.
Monitor it, and suspend it and tell the provider if it poses a risk.
Keep the logs it generates for at least six months.
Tell people when AI helps make decisions about them.
Explain the decision to an affected person who asks.

rules.note: Applies from 2 Aug 2028 (moved from 2 Aug 2027 by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744). Machinery now sits in Annex I Section B and is handled through the Machinery Regulation. Whether a product needs third-party assessment depends on its sectoral law; check it.

rules.title: Annex III area, but not high-risk under the Art. 6(3) derogation

obligations.text: Document why it is not high-risk before release.
Register it in the EU database anyway.

rules.note: Judgement call: the derogation fails if the system materially influences decisions about people; if in doubt treat it as high-risk. Date follows the Annex III timeline. Stacks so the documentation duty is never lost under another tier.

obligations.text: Tell people they are talking to an AI, from the first message.
Under your own brand, you must show the AI notice yourself.

rules.title: AI-generated or manipulated content

obligations.text: Mark outputs as AI-generated in a machine-readable way.

rules.note: Generative systems already on the market before 2 Aug 2026 have until 2 Dec 2026 (Art. 111(4) as amended).

rules.title: Emotion recognition or biometric categorisation disclosure

obligations.text: Tell people emotion recognition or biometric sorting is in use.

rules.note: Not returned when the use is prohibited under Art. 5(1)(f) or (g).

obligations.text: Clearly disclose that the content is AI-generated or manipulated.

rules.title: AI text on matters of public interest

obligations.text: Disclose that the text is AI-generated or manipulated.

rules.title: AI literacy

obligations.text: Train staff who run or use the AI, and keep a record.

rules.note: Applies to every provider and deployer. Wording softened by Reg. (EU) 2026/1744; no specific literacy level is required.

rules.title: General-purpose AI model provider

obligations.text: Keep technical documentation of the model.
Give downstream providers the information they need to comply.
Have a copyright policy that respects opt-outs from data mining.
Publish a summary of the training content.
If you are outside the EU, appoint an authorised representative in the EU.

rules.note: Models already on the market before 2 Aug 2025 must comply by 2 Aug 2027. Commission fines enforceable from 2 Aug 2026. Open-source models get partial relief (Art. 53(2)) unless systemic risk.

rules.title: General-purpose AI model with systemic risk

obligations.text: Notify the Commission when it crosses the systemic-risk threshold.
Test the model adversarially and mitigate systemic risks.
Report serious incidents to the AI Office quickly.
Keep adequate cybersecurity for the model and its infrastructure.

rules.title: GDPR: lawful basis, transparency and security

obligations.text: Pick and record a lawful basis for using the personal data.
Tell people what data you use, why, for how long, and that AI is involved.
Use only the personal data you need, and keep it no longer than needed.
Let people access, correct and delete their data, and object.
Keep the personal data secure (access control, encryption, logging).
If you use the data for your own purposes, such as training or improving the model, you are a controller for that and need your own lawful basis and notice.

rules.note: GDPR applies alongside the AI Act (AI Act Art. 2(7)). The GDPR changes in the Digital Omnibus proposal COM(2025) 837 are not adopted; this follows the GDPR in force. Mapping: the AI Act deployer is usually the GDPR controller; the AI Act provider is a processor when it runs the system on customers' data, and a controller for anything it does for its own purposes (e.g. training). Not returned when the AI Act prohibits the use.

rules.title: GDPR: AI vendors as processors

obligations.text: Have a data processing agreement with every AI vendor that handles the personal data for you.
If the data leaves the EEA (e.g. a US model API), use a transfer tool such as the EU-US Data Privacy Framework or SCCs.
When you run the system on a customer's personal data, act only on their documented instructions under a data processing agreement.
Get the customer's approval for sub-processors (e.g. your model API) and flow the same terms down.
Help the customer with data subject requests, breaches and DPIAs, and delete or return the data at the end.

rules.note: A provider that uses customer data beyond the customer's instructions becomes a controller for that processing (Art. 28(10)). Mapping: the AI Act deployer is usually the GDPR controller; the AI Act provider is a processor when it runs the system on customers' data, and a controller for anything it does for its own purposes (e.g. training). Not returned when the AI Act prohibits the use.

rules.title: GDPR: data protection impact assessment

obligations.text: Do a data protection impact assessment before you start, and review it when the system changes.
If high risk remains after mitigation, consult the data protection authority before starting.
Give deployers the information about the system they need for their DPIA.

rules.note: Conservative: triggered by any AI Act high-risk area, profiling, solely automated significant decisions, or special-category data (Art. 35(3) and the DPC's list of high-risk processing). A FRIA can reuse the DPIA (AI Act Art. 27(4)). Mapping: the AI Act deployer is usually the GDPR controller; the AI Act provider is a processor when it runs the system on customers' data, and a controller for anything it does for its own purposes (e.g. training). Not returned when the AI Act prohibits the use.

rules.title: GDPR: solely automated decisions with significant effects

obligations.text: Only make these decisions if needed for a contract, allowed by law, or with explicit consent.
Let people get a human to review the decision, give their view and contest it.
Explain the logic involved and the likely consequences to the people affected.
Build in a way for a human to review and overturn individual decisions.

rules.note: Easiest fix is often real human review of each decision, which takes it out of Art. 22. Special-category data in these decisions needs explicit consent or substantial public interest (Art. 22(4)). Mapping: the AI Act deployer is usually the GDPR controller; the AI Act provider is a processor when it runs the system on customers' data, and a controller for anything it does for its own purposes (e.g. training). Not returned when the AI Act prohibits the use.

rules.title: GDPR: special-category data

obligations.text: Have an Art. 9(2) condition (e.g. explicit consent) on top of your Art. 6 lawful basis.
Apply stronger safeguards to this data: restricted access, encryption, short retention.
Only use special-category data to detect and correct bias under the strict AI Act conditions.

rules.note: Biometric data counts as special category only when used to uniquely identify someone; emotion recognition alone may not be. Treat as special if unsure. Mapping: the AI Act deployer is usually the GDPR controller; the AI Act provider is a processor when it runs the system on customers' data, and a controller for anything it does for its own purposes (e.g. training). Not returned when the AI Act prohibits the use.
